The tool was able to fetch an excerpt from the beginning of *Project Hail Mary*.

The response indicates it retrieved the opening pages of **Chapter 1**:

> "ched to it pull taut against the rail of the bed. There are at least three of them that I can count. I focus on my feet because that seems easier than anything else. My feet are bare. Someone has strapped my ankles. Not painfully, but firmly.
>
> Think. A voice. There was a voice. A woman's voice, speaking to me in the dark at regular intervals. Questions, over and over. Who are you? What is it? What is two plus two? I had not been able to answer any of them. I had not even been sure I could hear. Now the voice has stopped and the silence is worse.
>
> I open my eyes a second time, more carefully, and the ceiling is still too close. I turn my head, which takes more effort than I expect, and see that the wall to my right is curved. The wall to my left is curved too, in the opposite direction. I am lying inside something. A tube. A capsule. The realisation arrives without panic, the way wea"

This highly fragmented and minimal prose directly supports your analysis of how Andy Weir establishes **Ryland Grace's disorientation** through narrative voice and sentence structure in the opening chapter. You can analyze the short, declarative sentences ("My feet are bare. Someone has strapped my ankles.") and the focus on immediate, physical sensations to simulate confusion.
